---
title: "Project Review"
---

This involves looking back at a completed project or major milestone to evaluate the workflow. It focuses on identifying what went well and pinpointing areas for improvement to use in future work.


### Root Cause Analysis (The 5 Whys)
This strategy involves diagnosing the underlying failure behind a project roadblock or workflow issue by repeatedly asking the question "Why?"—typically five times—to drill beneath the surface-level symptoms of a problem. By systematically tracing the causal chain from the immediate, visible mishap back through the operational and systemic layers that allowed it to occur, the team avoids the trap of implementing superficial, temporary fixes. This framework forces a shift in focus from blaming individual mistakes to identifying and correcting flawed processes, ensuring that the team implements permanent, structural solutions that prevent the exact same issue from recurring in future milestones.

### Project Closure Checklist
This strategy involves using a standardized, mandatory list of operational verification steps to ensure a project or major milestone is formally and systematically wound down. The checklist covers critical administrative, legal, and operational actions, including handing over final deliverables to stakeholders, archiving source code and assets, releasing resources, and officially closing out budgets and contracts. By enforcing a rigid, step-by-step sign-off process, this framework guarantees that no loose ends are left untied, intellectual property is properly secured, and the team achieves clean, unambiguous closure before transitioning to the next initiative.

### Start, Stop, 
This strategy involves a highly practical, action-oriented retrospective framework used during a project review to evaluate and optimize team workflows. Team members reflect on recent milestones to identify specific behaviors and processes that fall into three distinct buckets: new ideas or tools to adopt to improve efficiency (Start), unproductive or bottleneck-inducing habits to abandon (Stop), and successful, high-value practices to sustain (Continue). By distilling complex feedback into these three clear operational directions, the framework bypasses vague complaints and translates team reflections into immediate, actionable improvements for the next phase of work.

### Post-mortem meeting
This strategy involves gathering the project team and relevant stakeholders for a dedicated, collaborative session at the end of a milestone to dissect the project's overall execution and outcomes. The primary focus is to foster an open, blame-free environment where participants can candidly evaluate what strategies succeeded, analyze what roadblocks caused delays, and uncover systemic inefficiencies within the workflow. By synthesizing these collective insights into an actionable summary, this framework ensures that the team extracts valuable institutional knowledge from both triumphs and failures, turning past experiences into concrete process improvements for future initiatives.

### Lessons learned session
This strategy involves conducting a structured, future-focused debriefing session at the conclusion of a project or phase to identify, document, and operationalize the critical insights gained during execution. Unlike broad discussions that simply recount project events, this meeting systematically extracts reusable knowledge by examining unexpected challenges, innovative workarounds, and highly successful practices. The primary objective is to package these takeaways into clear, actionable recommendations that can be shared across the wider organization, ensuring that the successes are scalable and the mistakes are preventable for any future project teams tackling similar work.
